books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Figures from Barron’s Premium AP U.S. History 2027, Chapter 7 (about $2.6 billion borrowed, about $400 million from individual savers; Legal Tender Acts 1862–1863; National Bank Acts 1863–1864; first income tax 1861) and the Gilder Lehrman Institute (about $450 million in greenbacks issued). Figures are rounded.
stimulus.text:
How the Union paid for the war (approximate figures).

| Measure | What happened |
| Borrowing | About $2.6 billion in bonds sold; about $400 million of the bonds were bought by individual savers |
| Greenbacks | About $450 million in paper money issued under the Legal Tender Acts of 1862–1863 |
| Taxes | First federal income tax levied in 1861; rates stayed modest |
| National banking | National Bank Acts of 1863–1864 created a national banking system |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The table notes the first federal income tax, levied in 1861. The income tax mattered less as a source of money than bonds did, because

options.text: the tax was never actually collected from anyone.
options.misconception: Background: the wartime income tax was collected; it expired in 1872 rather than going uncollected.

options.text: only Southern states paid it, and never the North.
options.misconception: Background: the tax was levied by the federal government in the loyal states; the Confederacy had its own taxes.

options.text: the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional in 1861.
options.misconception: Background: the wartime income tax was not struck down; the income tax of 1894 was struck down in 1895.

options.text: rates stayed modest, and borrowing supplied far more of the cost.

rationales.A: Background: the wartime income tax was collected; it expired in 1872 rather than going uncollected.
rationales.B: Background: the tax was levied by the federal government in the loyal states; the Confederacy had its own taxes.
rationales.C: Background: the wartime income tax was not struck down; the income tax of 1894 was struck down in 1895.
rationales.D: Rates stayed modest in the face of public opposition, and borrowing supplied far more of the war’s cost than the new income tax did.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the rows: bonds run to about 2.6 billion dollars, while taxes are described as modest.
2. A first tax is a toe in the water, not a flood.
3. Background: the public opposed high wartime taxes, so Congress kept rates low.
4. The government therefore leaned on borrowing, and asked ordinary savers to buy bonds.
Remember: the biggest row in a money table is usually the one that carried the war.
